crux.for_the_english: he must never become quaint Cockney or stage-Japanese. Use dropped, run-on, self-interrupting colloquial syntax, repetitions and verbal tics in place of the sentence-ending な and the self-deprecating でげす forms, and let the dignity show through competence and generosity, not through making his grammar more respectable.
crux.point: keep Nekohachi's patter as work, not local colour
crux.why: His banter on the tram in p2-p10 is not decoration before the serious part begins; it is the act itself, carried on in public because passengers have become an audience and a comeback is professionally compulsory. Again at the meeting he tests jokes, misapplies the borrowed word "situation" (p67-p69), apologises, recovers, and feels the flatness when は、は、は does not come (p63). If English tidies this into witty repartee it ennobles him; if it renders it as broad dialect comedy it does to him exactly what his audiences do.

crux.for_the_english: do not iron out the long, associative sentences in which cabbages, a bath, a fee and a son succeed one another, and do not cut the lists. Keep the repetitions - animals, vegetables, children, money - as repetitions: they are Berman's networks, the web the story is made of, not redundancy to be varied away.
crux.point: keep the ramble, because the ramble is the consciousness
crux.why: The narration stays glued to Nekohachi's mind, and that mind does not proceed: on the tram it slides from a heckle to why a comedian must not laugh, to protecting a voice he does not drink for, to caterpillars in a ditch and cutworms that, like thieves and like himself, work only at night (p10-p14). The garden returns at every pressure point (p20, p31-p33, p100, p158, p172-p173) and is still what he offers the departing gentlemen at his own gate (p182). A fluent version that breaks this into themed paragraphs, or clarifies the transitions, has rationalised away the man.

crux.for_the_english: keep the embedded summary flat and a little long-winded, keep its pathos unlyrical, and keep Nekohachi's interventions in his own terms (a father should not let the child see it) rather than translating them into the group's critical vocabulary. Let the reader feel the identification before Nekohachi names 悲哀 for himself.
crux.point: let 'The Tiger' stay a clumsy paraphrase, not a set piece
crux.why: Half the story is a second-hand retelling of Kume's tale of a comic actor cast as a tiger whose child finds him weeping in the wings (p48-p90). It would be easy to polish this into a moving story-within-the-story. In the text it arrives as reported talk, interrupted, jargon-dusted (シチュエイション, バック), and judged thin by everyone present. Its power for Nekohachi is precisely that this mediocre fiction has got his life: four sons, a gifted twelve-year-old he has moved to the suburbs to keep away from the yose (p50, p93-p95). Prettify the paraphrase and his response looks disproportionate; sentimentalise his response and the literati's cool verdict loses its sting.

open_questions.question: How far to take Nekohachi's borrowed critical words? He picks up シチュエイション and uses it to mean something like a fix, then perhaps 'compromise' (p67-p69), asks after a novel's 落ち as if it were a rakugo punchline (p82), and hears バック/ハイケイ and こんにゃく問答 as pure sound (p118). Keeping the English words 'situation' and 'background' preserves the joke that he is mouthing English; explaining his misunderstandings in the text would clarify what the story leaves for the reader to infer.
open_questions.why_it_matters: This is where the class gap is audible. Over-explanation makes him stupid, under-explanation makes the passages merely opaque, and either choice decides how much the reader laughs at him rather than with him.

open_questions.question: What to do with the blanked names ○○○様 and ○○家 (p155, p159, p168)? The blanks are in the source: discretion about aristocratic patrons, performed in the telling. Silently filling, footnoting speculative identities, or smoothing them into 'a certain lord' would each change the effect; the blank itself is Nekohachi showing he knows how to behave in great houses.
open_questions.why_it_matters: The blanks mark the exact border between his world and the one that summons carriages for him. They are also part of his boasting: he has been to houses whose names must be withheld.

open_questions.question: How straight to play the revelation that Kume anonymously savaged his own story in a review (p103), which instantly converts Nekohachi into Kume's admirer (p104)? The group reads it as frivolity; Nekohachi reads it as 茶気, a performer's trick he recognises, and concludes the audience decides (p107-p108).
open_questions.why_it_matters: It is the one moment his professional judgement and the literati's may be pointing, from opposite sides, at the same thing. Playing it as simple irony rebukes him; playing it as simple insight rebukes them.

open_questions.question: Is the ending's humility (p185) a genuine change of heart, a mood of one in the morning that will not survive breakfast, or the last performance of the night, given to himself? He wants to embrace the tiger and weep (p175), is ashamed of his own relief at two yen (p177), and goes home resolved to make his wife taste an entertainer's sorrow (p188).
open_questions.why_it_matters: An English ending that resolves into renunciation or redemption betrays the text; so does one that undercuts him with open irony. The temperature of the last page is an editorial fork the reading cannot settle.

data.reading:
The crux of 『猫八』 is a man hearing his own life told back to him as somebody else's mediocre fiction, and being unable to say so in any language the room will accept. Nekohachi is a yose mimic, half-crippled by rheumatism for over a decade, who earns his living imitating cats fighting, birds, insects and latterly aeroplanes, and who has moved his family to an inconvenient suburb precisely so that his gifted twelve-year-old son will not watch him do it and will not become a second Nekohachi (p50, p95). Taken by the patron Takami to a writers' study group, he listens to a flat paraphrase of Kume's 「虎」, about a comic actor cast as a tiger, proud of the applause, and found after the curtain by his small son, crying in the costume: "the tiger and the human child wept together for a while in the shadow of the dark scenery" (p87). Everyone present agrees the piece is shallow, deft, thin in background. Nekohachi sits with one hand on the tatami and thinks it is about him. A translation stands or falls on whether that recognition lands without ever being upgraded into insight: he does not achieve self-knowledge in the story, he achieves a feeling - 悲哀, a word he has literally just learned from the man across the room (p56-p57) - and he carries it home past the sleeping tenement like something he has been paid in.

Everything follows from keeping the two registers unmerged. Nekohachi's spoken voice is Edo working patter: ingratiating, self-deprecating, built on な and でげす, forever turning a slight into a routine - the heckler on the tram must be answered because the other passengers have become an audience (p5-p10), the fat acquaintance must be greeted with 大山大将 and a lie about another engagement to save face (p23-p26), a lord's carriage must be met by borrowing a kimono from the blacksmith's wife and pretending to come back from the bath (p159). This is not colour; it is labour, and it is also evasion. Against it stands the literati's talk, abstract, loanworded and cool: シチュエイション, バック, 現実主義, 具体的, personality as the backing of a work (p103-p117). Nekohachi understands none of the terms and most of the substance. He thinks "situation" may mean a tight spot, which for him it does: he is はめられて, fitted into the patrons' favour until he can no longer move (p53). The translation must let the reader hear that he is misusing their words and meaning something truer with them, without a narrator stepping in to award him the point. Equally, the gentlemen must not be flattened into villains. They are mildly kind, mildly bored, they feed him餅菓子 instead of the drink he refuses, the host's wife talks gardens and children with him (p119-p120), Takami quietly presses two yen on him outside (p176) - and three of them walk out in the middle of the most honest story he ever tells (p161). Condescension here is structural, not snarling, and English that gives them sneers, or gives him a rebuttal, destroys it.

The narration is the third voice and the treacherous one, because it keeps slipping into Nekohachi's own idiom and self-justifications: the long tram reverie that moves from why a comedian must not laugh, to the voice he protects by not drinking, to green caterpillars shaken into a ditch and stamped on (p10-p13); the sudden boilerplate of Edo pride, no money kept overnight, born in Asakusa to a geisha mother (p158), set down right beside the admission that he beats his wife for trying to save (p175). The narrator neither endorses nor corrects any of this. That evenness is what a fluent draft will most want to fix, by making the interior passages lyrical where the story turns sad and brisk where it is comic. Resist it. The prose should stay dogged, repetitive and faintly garrulous even at p175, when he wants, in hiding, to embrace the tiger and weep for a while: the bathos is the emotion, and ennobling it into a climax would be the exact falsification the story is about.

Against the stage the text sets the allotment, and it must be translated as seriously as the tiger. Digging a ditch along the rows so the caterpillars roll in (p12), watching for cutworms that work nights as he does (p13), worrying on the tram home that two or three seedlings' roots will be cut before he gets back (p20), the surplus cucumbers and aubergines he gives away (p11, p182): this is the one place he is competent without being laughed at, and the one generosity nobody applauds. Note that he ends the evening not with a resolution to quit - he does wish, at p177, that he could stop tomorrow - but by advertising his vegetables to the departing writers at his own dark gate, and planning to make his wife taste what he has felt (p182-p188). The shape is a long evening that changes nothing except the temperature of a man's self-pity, and translations that sharpen it into an arc of awakening will have imported the 落ち he himself kept asking for and was laughed at for expecting (p82-p85).

Repetitions are load-bearing throughout: the animal catalogue that runs from tiger, monkey and pig (p179) through his frog-origin story (p141-p145) to the firefly and the colic-worm he cannot imitate and blusters about (p147-p153); the children and the dreaded second Nekohachi; the fee that must never be named and is always on his mind (p171, p175-p177); the 気違いか猫八のような化け物 of the opening joke (p6), madmen and monsters as the only residents of Sugamo, which the whole story quietly tests. Keep them unvaried. Keep his set-pieces - the caged nightingale, the valley-crossing, the mating cranes, the earthworm research that got him taken for a burglar (p62, p124-p130) - as performance, with the room's inadequate laughter left inadequate. And keep the unglamorous furniture: Kōdan Club magazine, the gas lamp he has petitioned to advertise himself with (p186), the leftover cakes in his pocket with the borrowed magazines. This is a Taishō naturalist story whose pity works by inventory, not by statement.

voice_takes.label: close, warm, and performed - the house recommendation
voice_takes.line: Narration in plain, slightly long-winded English that keeps slipping into Nekohachi's own turn of phrase without quotation marks or apology; it reports his self-flatteries (Edo-born, money never kept overnight) in the same tone as his seedlings, and never steps back to judge either. Nekohachi himself in dropped, wheedling, run-on speech, all apologies and 'now, look here' and sentence-final appeals for agreement, quickening into pure act - sound-words, animal cries, abrupt changes of face - when he performs; his seriousness should keep breaking the patter rather than replacing it. The literati in complete, abstract, faintly bored sentences, polysyllabic where he is monosyllabic, kind in the way of people who will not be there at the end of the sentence. Takami a register between: clubbable, easy, the only man who speaks both languages. Wrong for this take: dialect spelling, music-hall Cockney, 'gee' and 'ain't' folksiness, or any lyric lift at the tiger's climax - the moment the English gets beautiful, it has joined the study group against him.

voice_takes.label: drier and more naturalist
voice_takes.line: Narration flatter and cooler, closer to reportage, letting the inventories of the tenement, the allotment and the evening's talk accumulate without warmth, so that Nekohachi's bursts of patter stand out as noise he makes against a quiet world. His speech still colloquial but less lovable - more repetitive, more importunate - and the literati barely differentiated from one another, a single murmur of educated dismissal. This take risks seeming to side with the room, but it honours Iwano's naturalism and makes the final walk home colder and less consoling. Wrong for it: any softening of the wife-beating admission or the fee anxiety, which this take needs unglossed to work.

voice_takes.label: more theatrical, playing the act
voice_takes.line: Narration keeps pace with a performer thinking: quicker cuts, jokes left to land or die in the spacing, the animal imitations given real stage room with their onomatopoeia carried over, and the study-group scenes played almost as dialogue in a play, Nekohachi a comic turn among tragedians. His origin story on the Yoshiwara embankment becomes the bravura centre it is in his own mind. This take is the most readable aloud and the most dangerous: it flatters exactly the gift the story is examining, and will need discipline to keep the garden passages, the walkouts and the two yen as heavy as the applause. Wrong for it: punchlines sharpened beyond the source, or pathos borrowed back from the tiger to pay for the comedy.
